(A) Before 1662 the group had no official building, so its members met informally once a week in different places: at Dr. Goddard's house in Wood Street, at the Bull's Head Tavern in Cheapside, and at Gresham College. The circle also brought together men from many fields, including mathematics (Wallis), astronomy (Foster), and medicine and physiology (Goddard, Glisson), so knowledge was shared across subjects at these regular meetings.

(B) One development was Francis Bacon's argument, in works like the Novum Organum (1620), that knowledge of nature should come from careful observation and experiment instead of from ancient authorities like Aristotle. Bacon said this kind of research was too big for one person and needed many investigators collecting and comparing results. That is why scholars like those in the excerpt met as a group to do experiments and discuss what they found.

(C) A difference shows up in the Ottoman Empire, where astronomy was organized by the state. Sultan Murad III paid for an observatory in Istanbul run by Taqi al-Din in the late 1570s, and the state also had it torn down in 1580. The London circle, by contrast, was a voluntary group of private scholars meeting in homes and taverns, so its work did not depend on one ruler's support and could not be shut down in the same way.

Between 1200 and 1750 states and communities responded to famine, disease, and environmental stress in many ways. Some things changed and some things stayed the same, so the responses changed to a certain extent but also kept continuity. This essay will look at both change and continuity in how people dealt with these problems.

During this time there were many crises. There was the Black Death in the 1300s and the weather got colder in what is called the Little Ice Age. Many people died and harvests failed in a lot of places, so rulers and communities had to figure out what to do.

One response was storing grain. In China the government used granaries to keep food for bad years, and this kept going for a long time, so it shows continuity. People also turned to religion and charity when things got bad, since they believed God or the gods could help with disease and hunger.

Another response was quarantine. In 1377 the city of Ragusa made ships wait thirty days before people could come ashore because of plague. This was a new idea compared to just praying, so it shows change. Over time more cities copied this kind of thing.

In conclusion, responses to famine and disease changed some because of new ideas like quarantine, but they also stayed the same in other ways like storing grain. Overall there was both change and continuity between 1200 and 1750.

Between 1200 and 1750 responses to famine, disease, and environmental stress changed somewhat, but many older methods stayed in use. States kept relying on stored grain and on controlling labor, while new ideas like quarantine appeared after the plague. I will show this by looking at responses to the Black Death and then at responses to famine.

The Black Death in the 1300s was a huge crisis that spread along trade routes across Afro-Eurasia, which were connected by the Mongol empire. This killed a very large share of the people in many places and forced governments to react.

One response was in England. In 1349 the English government issued the Ordinance of Labourers. After so many workers died, wages went up because there were fewer peasants to do the work. The ordinance said that workers had to accept the wages that were paid before the plague and could not refuse to work. This was a way for the king and landlords to keep control of labor. Later, in 1351, the Statute of Labourers repeated these rules. So the government answered the disease by making laws about workers instead of helping the sick.

A different response happened in the city of Ragusa on the Adriatic coast. In 1377 Ragusa made a rule that travelers coming from places with plague had to wait thirty days in isolation before entering the city. Later the waiting time grew to forty days, which is where the word quarantine comes from. This was a new way of dealing with disease because it tried to stop the sickness from spreading by separating people.

For famine, states in many places continued to use granaries. In China the government used ever-normal granaries to store grain and sell it cheaply when prices were high. This was something that had been done for a long time before 1200 and kept going afterward. Religious institutions and villages also kept helping the poor with charity and prayer.

In conclusion, there was some change because of quarantine, which was new, but there was also a lot of continuity because granaries and labor control stayed important. The responses of England and Ragusa show that different places did different things, and the Chinese granaries show that old methods lasted. Overall the responses changed a moderate amount from 1200 to 1750.

input.essay:
Between 1200 and 1750, states and communities responded to famine, disease and environmental stress with a mix of old and new methods. Responses changed significantly in that governments after the Black Death began using more organized tools like quarantine, labor laws and new crops from the Columbian Exchange, but there was also strong continuity because states still relied on stored grain and religious explanations, and many responses were really about keeping control of labor and protecting the ruler's legitimacy.

In the 1200s and 1300s the Mongol Empire connected much of Afro-Eurasia through trade routes like the Silk Roads. This made it easier for goods and people to move, but it also helped spread the bubonic plague from Central Asia to the Middle East and Europe in the 1340s. Later the Little Ice Age brought colder weather and bad harvests to many regions, especially in the 1600s. At the same time, bigger empires with bureaucracies, like Ming and Qing China and the Tokugawa shogunate, had more ability to collect and redistribute resources, so they could respond to crises on a larger scale than earlier states.

One change was in how societies dealt with epidemic disease. When the Black Death first hit, many people saw it as punishment from God. Flagellants whipped themselves in public, and in some places Jews were blamed for poisoning wells and were attacked or killed. These responses were religious and based on scapegoating. But some cities began trying more practical methods. In 1377 Ragusa (Dubrovnik) required travelers coming from plague areas to be isolated for 30 days before entering, and later this became the 40 day quarantine used by Venice and other Italian cities. This shows a change toward state-run public health, although religious processions and prayers continued alongside quarantine, so the old response did not disappear.

Labor laws also show how governments responded to crisis in a way that protected the elite. After so many peasants died, workers in England demanded higher wages. The Ordinance of Labourers of 1349 tried to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and force people to work. This was a response to disease, but it was mainly about keeping landowners in control. A similar connection between crisis and labor control happened in the Americas after 1492. Smallpox and other diseases from the Columbian Exchange killed a huge part of the Indigenous population. In the Andes, the Inca had used mit'a labor to fill storehouses that fed people in bad years, but the Spanish turned the mita into forced labor at the silver mines of Potosi, and they resettled surviving Indigenous people into new towns so they were easier to tax and use for labor. So the Spanish kept an older system but changed its purpose from relief to extraction.

Food crises show the most continuity. Chinese dynasties had kept ever-normal granaries for centuries, buying grain when it was cheap and selling it when it was expensive, and the Qing continued this into the 1700s because providing relief supported the idea of the Mandate of Heaven. The Inca storehouses had a similar purpose of making the state look like a provider. What changed was the crops available. After the Kyoho famine in the 1730s, the Tokugawa government promoted sweet potatoes, a crop that originally came from the Americas, because they grew well in poor soil. New World crops like maize and sweet potatoes also spread in China and helped the population grow.

Overall, responses to crisis changed a lot in their methods, as quarantine, American crops and new labor systems appeared, but the goals behind them stayed similar. Rulers wanted to keep order, control workers and show they deserved to rule, which is why granaries and religious responses lasted even as new tools were added.
